item.prompt: Which stream property specifically describes a stream's ability to move the largest individual particle size (for example, cobbles)?
item.solution: Competence is defined as the maximum particle diameter a stream can transport. Capacity refers to the total amount of sediment carried, while discharge and velocity influence transport but are not the property that defines the maximum particle size. Therefore the correct choice is Competence.

reasoning_plan.target_skill: identify which stream property controls the largest particle size a stream can transport
reasoning_plan.novel_context: generic classroom scenario (no image required): students compare defined stream properties to decide which describes the ability to move large clasts
fixed_givens: Stream discharge = volume of water passing a point per unit time (m^3/s); higher discharge generally increases flow velocity and turbulence.
Velocity = speed of water in the channel (m/s); higher velocity increases the force available to move sediment.
Competence = the maximum particle diameter (size) that a stream can move (e.g., sand, gravel, cobbles).
Capacity = the total mass or volume of sediment a stream can carry (regardless of individual particle size).
Bed load = coarse particles that move by rolling, sliding, or short hops along the bed; requires high shear stress to move.
Suspended load = finer particles kept aloft by turbulence.
Dissolved load = solutes carried in solution; not related to particle transport size.

item.prompt: Top of map = north. Water-table contour lines (m above sea level) are shown as follows: 152 m in the northwest, 150 m in the north-central area, 148 m just north of point P, 146 m just south of point P, and 144 m along a meandering stream that lies east of point P. Point P is midway between the 148 m and 146 m contours and is 100 m west of the stream (stream stage = 144 m). The stream is hydraulically connected to the aquifer. Groundwater flows from higher head to lower head approximately perpendicular to water-table contours toward lower values. Given these conditions, toward which compass direction is groundwater most likely flowing at point P?
item.solution: Contour values decrease toward the southeast (148 m north of P → 146 m south of P → 144 m at the stream east-southeast of P). Flow is roughly perpendicular to contours toward lower head, so at P groundwater will move toward the lower 144 m area, i.e., southeast.

item.prompt: A straight channel is sampled at three downstream stations: 0 km (Q = 4.0 m^3/s, v = 0.4 m/s), 5 km (Q = 12.0 m^3/s, v = 0.9 m/s), and 15 km (Q = 24.0 m^3/s, v = 1.6 m/s). Bed slope and sediment supply are roughly constant. Which type of transport shows the largest relative increase in amount carried from 0 km to 15 km?

choices.A: Bed load (coarse particles rolling/sliding on the bed)
choices.B: Suspended load (fine particles held in the water column)
choices.D: Stream capacity (total sediment mass the stream can carry)

item.solution: Discharge increases sixfold (4 → 24 m^3/s) and velocity increases fourfold (0.4 → 1.6 m/s), so turbulence and transport capacity rise substantially downstream. Suspended load is most sensitive to increased turbulence and velocity because finer particles are kept in suspension much more readily as flow and turbulence grow; therefore suspended load will increase proportionally more than bed load (which requires higher shear to move coarse particles) or dissolved load (controlled mainly by chemical supply and weathering). Thus suspended load increases the most.

Measured average discharge rises steadily from 4.0 m^3/s at 0 km to 12.0 m^3/s at 5 km to 24.0 m^3/s at 15 km. Measured average flow velocity rises from 0.4 m/s at 0 km to 0.9 m/s at 5 km to 1.6 m/s at 15 km. Bed slope and sediment supply are approximately constant along the reach. Which type of transport shows the largest relative increase in amount carried between 0 km and 15 km?
fixed_givens: Discharge (Q) at 0 km = 4.0 m^3/s, at 5 km = 12.0 m^3/s, at 15 km = 24.0 m^3/s
Average velocity (v) at 0 km = 0.4 m/s, at 5 km = 0.9 m/s, at 15 km = 1.6 m/s
Bed slope and sediment supply remain approximately constant

Definitions: bed load = coarse particles moving along the bed (roll/slide/saltation); suspended load = fine particles held in the water column by turbulence; dissolved load = solutes carried in solution
As discharge and velocity increase, turbulence and transport capacity generally increase, favoring transport of finer particles in suspension and overall greater total load

item.prompt: A shallow 50-hectare drinking-water reservoir adjacent to cropland has developed frequent seasonal algal blooms over five years after upstream fertilizer use increased. The reservoir receives mostly diffuse surface runoff, has no major inflowing rivers, and a controlled spillway. Monitoring shows (1) nitrate + phosphate concentrations are now high enough to support frequent blooms, (2) daytime surface DO often exceeds 10 mg/L during blooms but pre-dawn DO < 3 mg/L (hypoxia) is now observed causing fish kills, (3) decomposition of dead algae consumes DO, and (4) average water residence time ≈ 90 days. Which single management action would most directly and effectively reduce the frequency of pre-dawn hypoxia (DO < 3 mg/L)?

choices.A: Install large mechanical surface aerators to continuously add oxygen to the water column.
choices.B: Reduce upstream fertilizer application and implement agricultural best-management practices to lower nutrient runoff into the reservoir.
choices.C: Dredge accumulated bottom sediments to remove nutrient-rich muck.
choices.D: Modify the spillway to increase water residence time so the reservoir flushes more slowly and algae settle out.

item.solution: Hypoxia is driven by high algal biomass from elevated nutrients; algal respiration and decomposition consume oxygen at night and after blooms. Removing the external nutrient driver (reduce fertilizer runoff and apply BMPs) lowers algal bloom magnitude and thus nighttime DO demand, addressing the root cause. Aeration (A) treats symptoms and is temporary/energy-intensive; dredging (C) may remove some internal stores but won't stop continuous external inputs and can resuspend nutrients; increasing residence time (D) would likely worsen in-reservoir algal growth and decomposition, increasing hypoxia risk.

reasoning_plan.target_skill: Identify the most effective management action to reduce hypoxia in a small eutrophic reservoir by applying cause-effect reasoning about nutrient inputs, algal blooms, and oxygen dynamics.
reasoning_plan.novel_context: A shallow 50-hectare drinking-water reservoir near agricultural land has shown seasonal algal blooms. Farmers increased fertilizer use upstream over the past five years. The reservoir has no major inflowing rivers; water enters mainly as diffuse surface runoff and exits via a controlled spillway. Monitored facts for the reservoir: (1) Dissolved nutrient concentrations (nitrate + phosphate) have risen from low to high enough to support frequent algal blooms. (2) During large blooms, daytime dissolved oxygen (DO) near the surface can exceed 10 mg/L, but pre-dawn hypoxia events (DO < 3 mg/L) are now observed and cause periodic fish kills. (3) Decomposition of dead algae consumes DO in the water column. (4) Average water residence time is about 90 days.
fixed_givens: Increased nutrient (nitrogen and phosphorus) concentrations stimulate algal (phytoplankton) growth.
Algal photosynthesis raises DO during daylight; algal respiration and microbial decomposition consume DO, especially at night and when algal biomass dies and decomposes.
Hypoxia is defined here as DO < 3 mg/L and causes fish stress and mortality.
Increasing water residence time (holding water in the reservoir longer) generally gives more time for algal biomass to accumulate and decompose in situ.
Dredging removes accumulated bottom sediments but is costly and may not remove dissolved nutrients already in the water column or upstream sources.
reasoning_plan.question_text: Which single management action would most directly and effectively reduce the frequency of pre-dawn hypoxia (DO < 3 mg/L) in this reservoir?

choices.A: Install large mechanical surface aerators to add oxygen to the water column continuously.
choices.B: Reduce upstream fertilizer application and implement best-management practices to lower nutrient runoff into the reservoir.
choices.C: Dredge sediment from the reservoir bottom to remove nutrient-rich muck.
choices.D: Modify the spillway to increase water residence time so the reservoir flushes more slowly and algae settle out.

nodes.label: Nutrient concentrations have increased enough to support frequent algal blooms.
Algal photosynthesis increases DO during day; algal respiration and decomposition consume DO at night and during decay.
Pre-dawn hypoxia (DO < 3 mg/L) events and fish kills are occurring following blooms.
Reducing nutrient inputs lowers algal biomass potential, which reduces magnitude of nighttime respiration and decomposition, decreasing hypoxia frequency.
Mechanical aeration adds oxygen directly and can temporarily raise DO but does not stop algal blooms or eliminate nutrient sources; may be energy-intensive.
Dredging removes some internal nutrient stores in sediments but is expensive and may not address continuous external nutrient inputs; resuspension can temporarily increase nutrients.
Increasing residence time gives algae more time to grow and decompose in place, potentially worsening hypoxia.
Select the most effective single action to reduce pre-dawn hypoxia frequency.

distractor_mechanisms: Choose mechanical aeration (A) assuming adding oxygen addresses root cause; this overlooks that aeration treats symptoms and is energy-intensive and temporary.
Choose dredging (C) believing sediment removal fully removes nutrients; this ignores ongoing external nutrient inputs and possible resuspension during dredging.
Choose increasing residence time (D) by misreading 'slower flush' as beneficial; in fact, longer residence often allows more algal growth and in-reservoir decomposition, worsening hypoxia.

verification.calculation: Conceptual justification: reducing external nutrient supply lowers algal bloom magnitude, thereby reducing nighttime respiration and frequency of DO < 3 mg/L events.
